title: Asia’s search for long-term, lower-carbon LNG supply puts Canada in focus but competition is intensifying
gist: LNG Canada's Phase 2 FID (September 2026, which doubles the facility to 28 mmtpa) puts Canada on track for about 33 mmtpa of exports by 2030, still far short of Carney's 100 mtpa goal, as Asian demand heads from 260 to about 500 mtpa by 2060 with much of it uncontracted. Wood Mackenzie and PETRONAS argue that Canada's proximity and low-carbon edge are offset by high costs and execution risk while US projects (CP2, Commonwealth, Delfin) win FIDs, and that the next 3-5 years of contracting will decide its share.

insights.claim: LNG Canada took a final investment decision on its Phase 2 expansion in September 2026, which doubles the facility's capacity to 28 mmtpa.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Phase 2 FID is the anchor event that makes Canada a credible scaled Pacific LNG exporter.

insights.claim: With LNG Canada Phase 2 plus Woodfibre LNG and Cedar LNG, both under construction, Canada expects to export about 33 mmtpa of LNG by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Around 33 mmtpa by 2030 sets a near-term floor for Canadian West Coast LNG volumes reaching Asia.

insights.claim: Even after adding Ksi Lisims LNG, Canada's LNG pipeline is far below Prime Minister Mark Carney's 'energy superpower' goal of 100 mtpa of export capacity, which implies roughly 60+ mtpa of projects that have not yet been identified or sanctioned.

insights.so_what: The political target is far ahead of the bankable project slate, so expect policy support (financing, permitting) aimed at closing the gap.

insights.claim: Because more and more LNG projects are competing for scarce capital to reach FID, Canada's chance to win a bigger slice of the next wave of global LNG supply may be limited in both time and scale.

themes.theme: Asian LNG demand and uncontracted volumes

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that Asian LNG demand will roughly double, from about 260 mtpa today to around 500 mtpa by 2060.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: About 240 mtpa of extra Asian demand underpins the long-run case for new Pacific-facing supply.

insights.claim: A large share of Asia's future LNG demand is still uncontracted, which leaves room for new suppliers to lock in long-term market access.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: New exporters still have room to sign long-term offtake, but that room shrinks as contracts get signed.

insights.claim: Much of Asia's LNG demand growth is expected to come from South and Southeast Asia, but these markets are very price-sensitive and cannot absorb high energy costs for long, so the main growth markets are also the ones that most limit high-cost supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Growth markets will reward exporters with low delivered costs, not just volume, which works against high-cost projects such as Canada's.

insights.claim: Repeated geopolitical disruptions have exposed the risk of relying on concentrated supply sources, so Asian governments, utilities and buyers now treat diversification across geography, counterparties and carbon intensity as a strategic priority.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Buyers may accept a premium for non-concentrated, lower-carbon supply, which favours new geographies such as Canada.

insights.claim: For LNG exporters, delivered-cost competitiveness is becoming as important as supply reliability and emissions performance, because Asian buyers want portfolios that balance security, affordability and sustainability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A low-carbon or security edge on its own will not win contracts unless delivered cost is also competitive.

themes.theme: Canada's value proposition to Asian buyers

insights.claim: Canada stands out to Asian buyers because it combines resource scale, Pacific Basin access, short shipping routes and lower carbon intensity, a combination that is increasingly rare in global LNG.
insights.speaker: Joshua Ngu
insights.so_what: Being physically close to Asia and having lower emissions are Canada's main advantages over US Gulf Coast and other Atlantic Basin supply.
insights.quote: Canada offers something that is increasingly rare in global LNG markets: a combination of resource scale, Pacific Basin access and a short shipping routes

insights.claim: Buyers set Canada's resource advantage against cost, timeline and execution risk compared with alternatives that are already further along, so getting projects delivered on time matters more than the size of the resource.
insights.speaker: Joshua Ngu
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for Canadian LNG is execution and cost, not geology.
insights.quote: buyers are also weighing cost, timeline and execution risk against alternatives that are already further advanced

insights.claim: In 2026 alone, CP2 LNG, Commonwealth LNG and Delfin FLNG 1 reached FID in the United States, while projects in Africa, Australia and Latin America are still moving toward sanction.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A wave of US FIDs is taking up Asian offtake demand and capital that Canada is also chasing.

themes.theme: Four-part de-risking agenda for Canadian LNG

insights.claim: High labour costs, heavy infrastructure needs and a constrained skilled-labour pool put Canadian LNG at a structural cost disadvantage against competing projects worldwide.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cost inflation and labour scarcity are the main threat to the economics of new Canadian LNG trains.
insights.quote: High labour costs, substantial infrastructure requirements and constraints in the skilled labour pool risk placing Canadian LNG at a disadvantage

insights.claim: To move Canadian LNG projects to sanction, the whitepaper calls for predictable, transparent and time-bound permitting, because regulatory uncertainty weighs on both investor and buyer confidence.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Permitting reform is a key policy lever to watch under the Carney government's LNG agenda.

insights.claim: The scale of capital needed for Canada's next wave of LNG may require government-backed financing mechanisms, credit enhancements and public-private partnerships to bring in institutional and international investors.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect state-backed credit support for LNG, which could give institutional capital a lower-risk way into Canadian LNG infrastructure.
insights.quote: government-supported mechanisms, credit enhancements and public-private partnerships

insights.claim: Long-term LNG relationships rest on government-to-government strategic partnerships and energy diplomacy as well as commercial contracts, so Canada needs deeper engagement with key Asian importing countries.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch for Canada-Asia bilateral energy agreements as leading indicators of new offtake contracts.
